summary: A 1974 description of the second version of the procedure call documents, a host-level protocol used in the NSW system. It is a slightly constrained version of the ARPANET host-to-host protocol, with changes affecting allocation, RFNM waiting and retransmission. See also RFC 684.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC announces a new edition of documents for the National Software Works. It maps the document set and tells readers where to begin.

subtitle: An announcement of the second version of the National Software Works procedure-call document set.

tldr.problem: The National Software Works project needed procedures for communication among its software modules.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC announces version 2 of a set of documents covering the Procedure Call Protocol, its helper packages, host-level communication, data formats, and example services.
tldr.outcome: The announcement says version 2 substantially differs from version 1 and replaces it and the informal intermediate documents. It invites comments.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 674's status as Unknown and records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC itself says this release supersedes the earlier PCP document set.

sections.title: A New Document Set
sections.content:
RFC 674 announces the second published version of documents for the National Software Works (NSW) and its Procedure Call Protocol (PCP). The authors say SRI developed PCP for communication between NSW modules and invite comments from the network community.

Version 2 is described as substantially different from version 1. It replaces version 1 and all intermediate PCP documents that had been distributed informally. The listed documents were available as NLS files and formatted text files.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors published a substantially revised edition of the NSW and PCP documents. They ask readers to send comments on the new set.

sections.title: The PCP Documents and Packages
sections.content:
The PCP document describes the virtual programming environment and the exchanges between processes. PIP provides procedures for calling, resuming, interrupting, and aborting remote procedures. PSP adds data-store operations, while PMP covers process creation, interconnection, and processor allocation.

Other documents cover data structure formats, inter-host and inter-fork communication, accounting and identification, files, batch jobs, remote job entry, debugging, tool-bearing host requirements, and mapping black boxes into PCP. The announcement describes the purpose of each document rather than reproducing its specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: PCP is the central document. Companion documents explain its helpers, low-level communication, and services such as files, batch work, and debugging.

sections.title: Where Readers Should Start
sections.content:
The HOST document proposes constraints on the regular ARPANET host-to-host protocol for NSW, affecting allocation, RFNM waiting, and retransmission. The announcement says this topic has little effect on the rest of the NSW protocols.

Readers are directed to the main PCP document first, then PIP, PSP, and PMP. The low-level format and IPC documents are primarily for implementers. The remaining documents describe particular packages and their operating-system or task context.
sections.plainLanguage: Start with the main PCP document to understand the design. Read the detailed format documents only when implementing the system.
